articles.title: How Microsoft outage hit South East trusts, councils and police
articles.summary: South East Coast Ambulance Service says its 999 and 111 services remained fully operational.
articles.body:
NHS trusts, councils and police in the south-east of England have been affected by the global Microsoft outage.

Microsoft 365 Services, including Teams, Outlook and Microsoft's artificial intelligence software Copilot, were hit by "connectivity problems" , but by about 14:00 GMT email queues were "approaching normal levels", the company said.

On Friday morning, NHS trusts across Surrey, East and West Sussex, and Kent reported issues receiving and sending emails, while some said patient inquiries and referral correspondences were also affected.

Patients had been urged to contact NHS trusts by phone and to continue to attend planned appointments.

Local authorities and Gatwick Airport also reported problems with emails, but Gatwick said it was operationally running as normal.

South Western Railway, meanwhile, which runs services through Surrey, says the outage is not affecting its trains.

However, it said if people were unable to access tickets with their email, they could get them through their app or website.

East Kent Hospitals University NHS Foundation Trust said: "Please continue to use services wisely.

"You can consult your GP or pharmacist for minor illnesses or injuries, and urgent treatment centres are also open.

"Please save our emergency departments for serious injuries or life-threatening conditions."

Trusts reported procedures and appointments were going ahead as planned.

Surrey and Borders Partnership NHS Trust said its 24/7 mental health crisis helpline was operating as usual.

"If you need urgent mental health support, please call 111 and select the mental health option or call 0800 915 4644," it said.

The NHS trusts in the south-east of England that said they were affected were:

Ashford and St Peter's Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust

Surrey and Borders Partnership NHS Trust

Epsom and St Helier University Hospitals NHS Trust

East Kent Hospitals University NHS Foundation Trust

Kent Community Health NHS Foundation Trust

Queen Victoria Hospital NHS Foundation Trust

University Hospitals Sussex NHS Foundation Trust

At about 16:00, Epsom and St Helier University Hospitals NHS Trust said its Microsoft systems were starting to return to normal, but responses to emails could be delayed for the next few days.

Kent and Medway Mental Health NHS Trust also said its email services had returned.

West Sussex County Council said its emails and some other systems were not working as usual.

The local authority's phone lines remained open, but it said some services could be unavailable.

Brighton & Hove City Council also urged residents to call as emails were affected.

Medway Council and Surrey County Council also reported issues with their emails.

Shortly before 16:00, East Sussex County Council said its email system was working again.

Kent County Council said many of its services and systems were operating normally, but some "inconsistencies" remained.

Surrey Police said it emails had been impacted by the outage, while Kent Police and Sussex Police confirmed its online reporting submissions were working again.

South East Coast Ambulance Service said its 999 and 111 services remained fully operational despite the outage disrupting some of its internal systems.

"Our call triage system and our computer-aided dispatch system, which we use to deploy ambulances, are unaffected and remain fully operational," it added.

"We have robust, well-rehearsed contingency plans in place to manage the disruption and are keeping the situation under review."

Kent Fire and Rescue Service said it was affected but its emails had returned.

articles.title: Grief reverberates through this church near the deadly Brooklyn collapse
articles.summary: Leonor Yupa dropped to her knees Thursday when a Spanish-language media reporter said her 22-year-old son was among eight people whose lives were claimed by...
articles.body:
Leonor Yupa dropped to her knees Thursday when a Spanish-language media reporter said her 22-year-old son was among eight people whose lives were claimed by the Brooklyn building collapse the day before.

"I want my son! I want my son!" the Ecuadorian mother cried in Spanish as family members tried to hold Yupa up and others who gathered at Bethesda Church of God in Christ assured her the reports were unconfirmed.

The agonizing cries of another woman who just lost her husband reverberated through the Brooklyn sanctuary across the street from the collapse. When the woman learned her husband's body was pulled from the debris Thursday morning, she collapsed and wailed her husband's name.

Family members gathered around the widow and formed a prayer circle.

Just outside the church, a nervous father also prayed. He was anxiously waiting to learn the fate of his son, a construction worker who has not been reachable since the collapse.

In the Flatbush neighborhood – home to a mix of immigrant communities – six adults and two children had died and over a dozen were injured after the three-story mixed-use building collapsed on Veterans Day, a day on which many families stayed home.

"I want to take a moment to remember those we have so senselessly lost," Mayor Zohran Mamdani told reporters Thursday. "These were our friends and our neighbors, parents and children, young families building their lives in our city, and immigrants from Mexico, Colombia, Ecuador, Trinidad, and beyond."

The day after the tragedy, residents and other bystanders crowded the sidewalk as construction equipment was used to removed debris and rubble from the site. Clothes still hung from a closet in an adjoining building where a wall came down during the collapse.

A heavy rain pelted the intersection of Flatbush and Bedford avenues, a multicultural enclave that is the heart of New York City's Caribbean diaspora. The names on signs of storefront churches and businesses – from bakeries, restaurants and beauty salons – reflect places like Jamaica, Haiti, Trinidad and Tobago, and more recently, newcomers from Mexico and Ecuador.

Among those killed Wednesday were three Colombian citizens, two Ecuadorian men and a 26-year-old Guatemalan man, officials from the countries announced.

In the aftermath of the collapse, local families, clergy and community groups gathered to support one another while demanding accountability for housing conditions and construction oversight in their predominantly Black and immigrant neighborhood.

On Wednesday night, Yupa and other relatives spent hours scouring hospitals throughout Brooklyn hoping to find her son, Gabriel Siguencia.

The family then visited the collapse site Thursday. Yupa shielded herself from heavy rain under the canopy of the church as a woman with a West Indian lilt alerted other bystanders nearby that she saw first responders pull a young child and a woman from the rubble.

Then came the news about Siguencia, who had arrived in New York from Ecuador only about a month ago and started working as a carpenter at the construction site adjacent to the building collapse about two weeks ago, according to uncles, cousins and family friends.

"He came to America looking for the same opportunities that people from all over the world come here for," said family friend Javier Ortega, who drove Siguencia's mother to the site from her home in Connecticut. "That's why he was working there."

Like many other families, Siguencia's loved ones awaited news about him across the street from the collapse site. Some, like the husband of a six-month pregnant woman rescued from the rubble, rejoiced as they received word their loved one was safe.

As the downpour intensified Thursday over the neighborhood known as "Little Haiti," a member of Bethesda Church of God in Christ invited Siguencia's family inside the warm vestibule.

Yupa, weeping, sat on a folding chair as a Haitian church member served her cups of water. As Yupa sobbed, family members surrounded her and Ecuadoran consular officials made calls trying to track down information.

Soft murmurs of "Hallelujah, hallelujah" spilled out from the church filled with Haitian worshippers on the other side of the vestibule doors.

"We all have to look out for each other in this country," said the woman who brought water to Yupa and the others. "It doesn't matter where you come from."

Another woman implored Yupa as she wept: "Go in the church and pray, please."

Time ticked by with a heaviness before officials with the Ecuadoran consul walked Yupa and her friends and family members several blocks in the heavy rain to a nearby YMCA, where relatives of the dead and missing had been gathering.

The consul general of Ecuador, Gicela Andrade Valens, later told reporters outside that authorities had confirmed Siguencia's death to his mother. Another Ecuadorian national, 26-year-old José Luis Caguana Cosquillo, was also killed.

"We express our deepest condolences to his family and loved ones, and we stand with them in profound solidarity in these moments of grief," the consulate said.

Colombia's consulate in New York said two Colombian children and one adult were killed in the collapse.

"The Consulate of Colombia in New York reiterates its most sincere condolences to the victims' families and loved ones," the consulate said.

'Nothing like this has ever happened in this neighborhood'

Pastor Alfred Justin Joseph's church, the Bethesda Church of God in Christ, became an open sanctuary for the injured, the anxious and the grieving.

"They were standing in the street. I let them in," Joseph said. "Thank God we have counselors in the church — people who do counseling for grief."

Various groups have streamed through his church, including a dozen people in the first wave. While some have since been escorted to a local YMCA or hotels, the church remains an epicenter of consolation and support.

As she heard the wailing of the young woman who lost her spouse in the collapse, Flatbush resident Joy Kerr led a prayer circle to offer some comfort in a moment of devastation.

Kerr walked into the church and found the young woman crying hysterically after learning that her spouse, a construction worker, was killed when the building came down.

Kerr listened to the woman sobbing for about half an hour and said, "No, I can't take this. I can't sit back and just watch her and listen to her cry so hysterically."

"In that moment, I knew she needed comfort," she said.

She gathered with the woman who had lost her spouse and those around them, and they began to pray.

"This is devastating," Kerr said. "Nothing like this has ever happened in this neighborhood, and we just need to come together and stay together as a community."

And Katie Stevens, a teacher who lives about a block from the building, sobbed after she watched first responders load body bags into a van Thursday morning.

"I care for my neighbors so much," Stevens told CNN. "I'm just so sad."

James Williams, a bricklayer who has lived in the neighborhood for 35 years, stood across the street from the wreckage site Thursday and recalled watching the building's walls cave in the day before.

One image reverberated in his mind: a woman climbing a now-exposed staircase as everything around her was crumbling.

"I don't know if she got out alive or not," he lamented. "To see that and not know what happened to her…I might have to go see a psychiatrist."

Williams said he knows multiple families affected by the collapse. A friend told him she had been texting with relatives at the site when it collapsed but had not been able to locate them at any local hospitals.

As grief rippled through the neighborhood, nonprofits and agencies including the Red Cross, NYC Human Resources Administration and World Central Kitchen helped shaken families with emergency shelter, supplies and updates about missing people.

As darkness fell over the collapse site Thursday night, amid thunderclaps and heavy rain, floodlights shone on a now-idle backhoe that had been excavating piles of debris, twisted metal and the pieces of what had been apartments into dumpsters.

Crews finished a marathon search through the rubble and determined there were no more survivors to be rescued, officials had said Thursday afternoon.

Under umbrellas, people hurried home after work, some stopping momentarily to look at the now-vacant space that had recently been home to many.

Across the street, a cluster of older women started gathering early for an evening service at Bethesda Church of God in Christ.

"This church happens to be a Haitian Creole speaking church, but the church is open to the entire community," said Florence Saint-Jean, a psychologist who offers mental health and trauma services at the church.

"The people who live here are immigrants, and so when crisis happens, there's only one language – love," she said. "People are tired, they're looking for food, they're looking for shelter, and the church is always open and available."

As neighbors hugged and comforted one another, one question created knots in their chests: How could this tragedy have happened?

The Department of Buildings has not yet determined the cause of the collapse, and an investigation is underway as new information emerges about the building's history and construction process.

New York officials are looking into what caused the collapse of the building built in 1930, with Mamdani vowing to hold anyone responsible "fully accountable" and authorities inspecting about 100 locations throughout the city linked to the site.

The Brooklyn District Attorney's Office is conducting its own investigation into whether laws were broken.

"We are working closely with the Department of Buildings and our law enforcement partners to determine whether any criminal conduct contributed to this tragedy," district attorney Eric Gonzalez said in a statement Thursday.

As investigators try to determine factors in Wednesday's deadly collapse of the three-story building in Brooklyn, they'll be looking at both the condition of the collapsed building and activity at the construction site that neighbored it.

Cracks had been reported in the facade of the building as part of the permitting process for construction on the adjacent lot, which the collapse spilled into.

The building's owner, Olufemi Falade , has a troubling history that reportedly landed him in jail for 12 days in 2006 for failing to repair hundreds of violations across multiple buildings.

The collapsed building at 1321 Flatbush Avenue currently has 98 open housing violations – ranging from unsafe electrical wiring and a lack of smoke detectors to bedbug infestations and a lack of adequate water supply for the building's sprinkler system – according to records from the New York City Department of Housing Preservation and Development. CNN has reached out to Falade for comment.

Though building collapses are rare in the US, lower-income and immigrant neighborhoods often face higher risks of hazards and neglect.

Housing experts and advocates have pointed to systemic inequities that disproportionately impact working class immigrant communities, including old buildings, lax code enforcement and rapid construction.

Sumathy Kumar, executive director of New York State Tenant Bloc and Housing Justice for All, an organization that works to organize tenants, said the Brooklyn landlord has an extensive and troubling history with the city.

"We need better and faster tools to hold landlords accountable and to make sure that buildings are properly maintained and managed," Kumar said.

Saint-Jean said there is a visible distinction between how development occurs in immigrant communities like Flatbush.

"What we're most concerned about is, when things like his happen, that our voice (is) not being heard about development in the area," she said.

CNN's Ray Sanchez reported from New York and Dalia Faheid from Los Angeles. CNN's Gloria Pazmino, Eduardo Cuevas, Brynn Gingras, Graham Hurley, Taylor Romine, John Miller and Holly Yan contributed to this report.

articles.title: More women make allegations against Russell Brand
articles.summary: The new claims are in the Times and a Netflix documentary, following Brand's recent conviction for rape.
articles.body:
Warning - this story contains graphic content

More women have come forward to make allegations about disgraced entertainer Russell Brand, in interviews with the Times and a new Netflix documentary.

Brand was jailed earlier this week after being found guilty of one count of rape and three of sexual assault at a trial in London.

Allegations against him first emerged after an investigation by the Times, the Sunday Times and Channel 4's Dispatches in 2023.

The Times has now reported accusations of what it called sexual misconduct and predatory behaviour by a further six women, which the newspaper said could not be reported until the criminal case had ended. He has denied non-consensual sexual activity.

The Times report was published on Thursday evening, and a Netflix documentary, titled Russell Brand: Open Secret, was made available on Friday morning.

The programme included an interview with a woman referred to as Emily, not her real name, who said she was in a relationship with Brand when she was in her twenties.

On one occasion, she said she "literally begged" Brand to stop after he refused to wear a condom during sex.

Emily, who was portrayed by an actress in the documentary, said: "I said to him, 'No, Russell, please, let's just use protection.' I kept saying 'No'. I said, 'Stop Russell, stop, please don't, please.'

"I begged him. I literally begged him. I tried to kick him off, I tried to draw my knees back, to kick him in his belly, but he was too strong for me."

But he "just pinned my hands back behind my head" before forcing himself upon her, she alleged.

"When it happens you just feel like, is this... is this rape? Because I'm with this guy [in a relationship]," she said, according to the documentary.

"I know I said 'No', but you question yourself and you think, did I do something wrong?"

She "left his as quickly as I could" and told one friend what had happened, but "back then women felt shamed", she said.

"You didn't talk about it. I just felt completely violated and unseen and unheard. I was saying 'No'. I kept saying, 'No, stop, please, stop, stop, no'."

Russell Brand being investigated over rape allegations from two more women, police say

Another ex-girlfriend, Jordan Martin, claimed in the documentary that Brand sexually assaulted her and smashed her phone in a hotel after she had spoken to an ex to arrange to collect her belongings.

"He snatched my phone out of my hand and broke it apart into pieces," she said.

Brand then followed her into a different room, she said. "He didn't say anything. He put his hand down the front of my jeans and he inserted a finger and then he walked away."

She added: "I look at myself back then and I feel sorry for myself. And not in a bad or pitying way, I just feel like it wasn't very fair."

Martin also said Brand was jealous and controlling, and had made her "brush her teeth until gums bled".

"He wanted me to taste anonymous," Martin said. "And so he was asking me to brush my teeth, but it just was never enough. And so he's standing over me and I'm brushing and I'm brushing, and then I'm seeing my teeth bleeding."

The Times and Sunday Times reported that at least five sexual partners said Brand had forced them to brush their teeth, including the fifth complainant in the trial, whom he was convicted of raping in 2009.

Among the new claims reported by the paper is one from a woman referred to as Alex, who claimed she had asked Brand to stop having sex after noticing he wasn't using a condom.

"I said, 'No, stop', and I started to sort of try and move. And... that wasn't happening," she said.

When he continued, she decided "I'm not going to fight", she said, because "who knows what he could do?"

Alex said Brand apologised in person and by text message after the alleged incident.

"I justified it in my head by saying to myself, at least he admitted it," she told the Times.

A woman called Vicky also claimed she had asked him to stop twice after they started having sex without any build up.

"My body wasn't ready for this and it was painful", she remembered.

"An uneasy wave hits me and I'm scared. And I say, 'It's painful' and he doesn't stop. And then it gets worse and it's really painful. And I say 'Stop' and he doesn't stop."

She added that it had felt like he "just wasn't present".

She claimed he said afterwards: "Tonight was consensual. Nobody did anything they didn't want to do."

Another woman named Zoe said Brand was "annoyed" after she turned up to his hotel late.

"He basically sort of just grabbed me and manhandled me around a little bit and he put his hand on my throat," she told the Times.

"And then he shoved his other hand down my trousers and penetrated me with his finger.

"I didn't resist. I just sort of let it happen."

On Monday, Brand was sentenced to 10 years and six months in prison following his trial. He is expected to serve seven years.

He denied the charges and was acquitted on two further rape charges and one count of attempted indecent assault.

Police have said Brand is being investigated over rape allegations made by two more women.

The Metropolitan Police have said they are also "assessing" information from several people who contacted them during the trial "to provide information or report a potential criminal allegation".

Brand has been placed inside HMP Wandsworth . BBC News has asked his legal representatives for a response to the latest allegations.

articles.title: Darth Vader’s lightsaber appeared in the ‘I Am Your Father’ duel; four decades later, the screen-used prop sold for $4.875 million, setting a Star Wars collectible record
articles.summary: A lightsaber used by Darth Vader in The Empire Strikes Back and Return of the Jedi sold for $4.875 million on Thursday, 12 November, a price that Heritage
articles.body: A lightsaber used by Darth Vader in The Empire Strikes Back and Return of the Jedi sold for $4.875 million on Thursday, 12 November, a price that Heritage Auctions says is a world record for any Star Wars collectible. The blade went under the hammer at the Ultimate Star Wars Auction held by the auction house that day.A record price surpassing previous highs for Star Wars collectiblesThe sale of the lightsaber has surpassed the auction house’s own previous record by about $1 million. That record was $3,875,000, paid for Tom Jung’s original half-sheet key poster painting for Star Wars: Episode IV – A New Hope. The lightsaber also set a new benchmark for screen-used Star Wars props. It surpassed the $3.75 million fetched by the auction house in July for Luke Skywalker’s lightsaber and severed-hand effects rig from The Empire Strikes Back.In fact, the auction house already held a record in another category. In 2023, its screen-matched Red Leader X-wing Starfighter, a filming miniature, sold for $3,135,000. The house has now set records in three of the most sought-after areas of Star Wars collecting.Darth Vader’s lightsaberThe lightsaber was used in the climactic duel on Cloud City, in which Vader tells Luke Skywalker, ‘I am your father.’ This iconic confrontation is one of the most replayed moments in the franchise, and it changed the direction of the saga. The blade also appeared in Return of the Jedi, linking it to the original trilogy’s final chapter.‘Vader’s weapon is a remarkable counterpart to that Skywalker lightsaber: both were used in the unforgettable Cloud City confrontation in The Empire Strikes Back, the duel that culminated in Vader’s revelation and changed the course of the saga. Its use in Return of the Jedi further connects the lightsaber to the original trilogy’s enduring legacy,’ Heritage said in a press release.The sale was part of an auction covering material from Episodes I through IX, as well as later films and television series. Vader’s weapon headlined what Heritage describes as the largest group of Star Wars lightsabers ever offered at public auction. Twenty-seven other examples accompanied it, representing many of the saga’s best-known Jedi and Sith.The sale reflects growing demand for screen-used film props. Collectors have been paying more for screen-used pieces for several years, and this result suggests that the trend is continuing. articles.title: Former Hamas bodyguard guilty of Birmingham knife attack
articles.summary: Mohammed Alfatih was granted asylum in the UK in 2015 and British citizenship in 2020.
articles.body:
A former Hamas bodyguard, wanted in Germany over an alleged plot to murder Jewish people, has been found guilty of a knife attack on a bailiff outside his UK home.

Mohammed Alfatih, previously known as Mohammed Naim, was regularly seen acting as a bodyguard for a former leader of Hamas in 2006. He was granted asylum in the UK in 2015 and British citizenship in 2020.

The 40-year-old was found guilty by majority verdict of unlawfully wounding a bailiff who had come to repossess his wife's car, possession of two knives and criminal damage. He was cleared of wounding with intent.

Alfatih was under surveillance by a counter-terror unit at the moment he attacked the bailiff in Birmingham last year.

The son of a senior Hamas official, he could not be named during his trial due to reporting restrictions.

During the trial, footage was shown of Alfatih brandishing two large kitchen knives outside his home in the suburb of Kings Heath and trying to stab the bailiff as he drove away.

He told the court he chased the victim across the street to scare him away after his wife was asked to settle her debts of more than £2,250 linked to unpaid parking fines.

Her car had been clamped by the enforcement officer, who was involved in a struggle inside Alfatih's terraced home.

Jurors were not told of Alfatih's links to proscribed terrorist group Hamas or his work as a bodyguard to its now-deceased former leader Ismail Haniyeh.

But it can now be revealed that while detained for the attack in Birmingham, he was re-arrested when authorities in Germany said he had been part of an alleged gun plot to attack Jewish targets there.

It is alleged Alfatih was an organiser and was involved in the movement of weapons.

German authorities also allege he had pre-recorded a video wearing a balaclava and sunglasses claiming the attack was planned on behalf of the Izzedine al-Qassam Brigades, the military wing of Hamas. The alleged attack was prevented after a tip-off from the Israeli intelligence agency Mossad.

Alfatih, who was born in Germany, is expected to be extradited to the country after he has served his sentence in the UK.

During his evidence, Alfatih did not mention Hamas but told the court he had been tortured for 25 days while detained in Egypt in 2010.

The father-of-four, an IT worker, failed in a legal application to try to get the wounding charges thrown out on the grounds of prejudicial media coverage about the investigation in Germany.

During the two-week trial at Birmingham Crown Court, the jury was shown video footage of Alfatih lashing out with a knife at the broken window of a van on 14 October last year.

Bailiff Kevin Bucknall was left with cuts to his head and required hospital treatment, but the defendant had pleaded not guilty on the grounds of self-defence.

Alfatih told jurors it had happened a day after he had learned one of his brothers had been killed in Gaza.

He also said while giving evidence that traumatic experiences in his past included being shot and injured on two different occasions.

"I just want to be as honest as I can," he told the jury.

"I don't think I was even in my full mind. I didn't intend anything other than him moving away.

"I wasn't anything more than terrified."

Defence barrister Kate O'Raghallaigh said Alfatih had a heightened perception of danger, triggered by fear and desperation he had previously experienced.

Jurors deliberated for more than six hours over three days before convicting him, with Alfatih heard mumbling to himself as the verdicts were returned.

He has been in custody since the knife attack and now faces sentencing in Birmingham on 11 January, as well as separate extradition proceedings at Westminster Magistrates' Court.

The BBC understands that when Alfatih went by the name of Naim, he enrolled in a VIP protection course and was selected to accompany Haniyeh on trips to Egypt and other countries between 2006 and 2008. However, he was later removed from the role due to his behaviour.

The second son of former Hamas health minister Bassem Naim, he later spent time in Malaysia, Qatar and Turkey before arriving in Britain.

Following his conviction, a government source said it was "staggering" that he was granted asylum and later given citizenship.

A Home Office spokesperson added Hamas was a proscribed terrorist organisation and the government condemned "those who choose to support its activities and further its aims".

articles.title: Reform could try to remove Senedd's presiding officer over speaking ban
articles.summary: The party's chief whip says it has not ruled out triggering a no confidence vote in Huw Irranca-Davies.
articles.body:
A senior Reform politician says a no-confidence vote in the Senedd's presiding officer is "not off the table", after a party member was banned for claiming white people are being "replaced".

Llŷr Powell, Reform's chief whip in Cardiff Bay, said his colleague Joe Martin had the right to raise "legitimate concerns" that were being "infringed upon".

Martin was told he would not be called to speak in the Welsh Parliament until he apologised for the remarks made on Tuesday, which Presiding Officer Huw Irranca-Davies called "unnecessarily provocative and deliberately offensive".

Reform withdrew from most Senedd proceedings on Wednesday in response.

Reform boycotts Senedd after member banned for saying white people are being replaced

Powell, who as chief whip enforces party discipline in the Senedd's Reform group, was asked on BBC Radio Wales Breakfast if his party would put forward a no confidence vote in Irranca-Davies.

He said: "I'm not going to say that we're going to do that now, but what I would say it's not off the table right now because freedom of speech and the right of members to raise legitimate concerns should be the main priority.

"And for us, right now, we see that as being infringed upon."

Powell denied Martin had made any connection to a far-right conspiracy theory that the white population was being deliberately replaced by the immigration of other ethnic groups.

"Joe was asking a legitimate question based on demographic changes," Powell said.

"The idea that he was framing some far-right theory is false.

"He was talking about legitimate concerns that is out there for data for all to see."

During business questions on Tuesday, Martin had asked Welsh government minister Heledd Fychan for a "statement from your government on the demographic replacement of white British people taking place in the UK".

"Mass immigration and differing birth rates mean that, in just 37 years' time, in 2063, we will be a minority in our own country," he said.

Fychan had asked the deputy presiding officer, who had been chairing the session, whether the question broke Senedd rules.

Irranca-Davies later called Martin's statement "unnecessarily provocative and deliberately offensive" and "clearly discriminatory" when he issued the speaking ban.

He said that unless Martin apologised to the Senedd chamber "we will not be calling him to speak".

Aliya Mohammed, chief executive of the charity Race Equality First, criticised Martin on Wednesday, saying "the idea that white people are being 'replaced' is linked to a conspiracy theory that creates division and wrongly portrays people from minority ethnic backgrounds as a threat".

Martin, a Member of the Senedd (MS) representing Caerdydd Penarth, was accused by Plaid Cymru of dangerous rhetoric in June when he claimed attacks from Sudanese asylum seekers were inevitable .

The next day MSs walked out during a speech where Martin joked that Welsh students were unable to read, and Indian nurses were taking Welsh jobs .

He was later accused by the presiding officer of making offensive remarks in a debate about the crisis-hit Welsh Gender Service .

Graham Laurie, a former pilot for Queen Elizabeth II, had said that William travelled with his parents and younger brother, Prince Harry, until he turned 12 in 1994. Exceptions were reportedly possible with the Queen's written permission.Questions have also been raised about William travelling with his family in helicopters. articles.title: Russell Brand accused by six more women of sexual misconduct
articles.summary: Allegations from the women have been published, including sexual assault, non-consensual sex, and controlling behavior spanning a decade.
articles.body:
Six more women have accused Russell Brand of sexual misconduct, according to an investigation by the Times and Sunday Times newspapers in London, days after the comedian was jailed for rape and sexual assault.

The claims made by the women, who all spoke under pseudonyms, span the period from 2005 to 2015.

Brand was sentenced to more than 10 years in prison on Nov. 9 after being found guilty of raping one woman and sexually assaulting three more between 2004 and 2009.

In new allegations published by the Times, one woman, who worked for Brand, claimed that he had non-consensual sex with her and that he apologized afterward.

The woman, identified as Alex, said she entered an on-and-off relationship with Brand after she met him at a work meeting in the 2000s. He later became controlling, she alleged, not letting her drink alcohol or eat meat in his company.

She alleged that, on one occasion during their relationship, Brand had non-consensual sex with her by not using a condom, despite her telling him to stop. She said Brand apologized in person and over text. "I justified it in my head by saying to myself: at least he admitted it," she added.

One woman using the pseudonym Vicky told the newspaper she met Brand as a 19-year-old fan after a 2007 comedy gig and alleges he ignored her repeated pleas to stop during a painful sexual encounter while another woman watched.

The woman claimed he said after the incident: "Tonight was consensual. Nobody did anything they didn't want to do."

The newspapers said journalists took "extensive steps" to corroborate the allegations, including speaking with friends and examining records of messages.

The allegations, which could not be reported until his criminal case concluded, come as the Netflix documentary Russell Brand: Open Secret was released today.

It features two of his former partners, including a woman identified as Emily, portrayed by an actor, who alleges Brand raped her.

Emily alleges that a younger Brand raped her during their relationship when she was in her late twenties and before he was famous. She says he overpowered her and had sex with her without her consent one morning after refusing her request to wear a condom.

In the documentary, a former girlfriend of Brand's, Jordan Martin, said he forced her to brush her teeth until her mouth bled, The Times reported.

"He wanted me to taste anonymous," Martin said. "And so, he was asking me to brush my teeth, but it just was never enough. And so he's standing over me and I'm brushing and I'm brushing, and then I'm seeing my teeth bleeding."

The Times said it had found at least five sexual partners who said Brand had forced them to brush their teeth.

Brand was sentenced to 10 and a half years in prison on Nov. 9 after he was found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault between 2004 and 2009.

He was acquitted of two rape counts and one count of attempted indecent assault.

Delivering the sentence at Southwark Crown Court in London, judge Joel Bennathan said Brand had acted with a "casual and arrogant disregard."

He said: "Whatever women wear, wherever they go, indeed whatever they drink, they retain the right to say 'no' and to demand justice from the criminal courts when sexual predators like you, Russell Brand, act without their consent."

London's Metropolitan Police force said after Brand was convicted that "several people" had contacted the investigation team during and since the trial to provide information or report a potential criminal allegation. Police said they were also investigating two further rape allegations.

The Times said Brand's representatives did not provide a substantive response to its latest allegations before publication. Responding to earlier allegations in 2023, Brand denied sexual wrongdoing and said his relationships had been consensual.

Yahoo News has contacted the Metropolitan Police and Brand's lawyers for comment.

articles.title: Russia hit by second car bomb in as many days as peace talks continue
articles.summary: A former adviser to Ukraine's pro-Putin ex-prime minister Mykola Azarov was seriously hurt, Russia says.
articles.body:
A car bomb in Moscow has injured a former adviser to Ukraine's pro-Putin ex-prime minister Mykola Azarov, Russia's Investigative Committee says.

Sergei Zavorotny was behind the wheel when the explosion happened on Friday morning. He was taken to hospital, investigators added.

Zavorotny had been an aide to Azarov until the prime minister resigned in 2014 and fled to Russia. The car bomb went off a day after a similar explosion killed a Russian colonel in Saint Petersburg.

It comes against a backdrop of peace talks in Dublin aimed at ending the war, although strikes by both Russia and Ukraine continued overnight.

Zelensky welcomes US bringing Europe into Russia-Ukraine peace talks

"Serhiy Zavorotny, a former adviser to the former Prime Minister of Ukraine Mykola Azarov, who was driving a car, was injured. He was taken to one of the city hospitals, where he is receiving medical care," a statement from the committee said on Telegram.

"A set of necessary investigative actions is being carried out. A number of examinations will be appointed, including medical and explosives."

Unconfirmed reports from Russia claim he has lost his left arm and suffered a brain injury, broken ribs and right leg.

On Thursday a car bomb in the Pushkinsky District of Saint Petersburg killed a member of the Russian military.

Russia say the car bombs are the latest in a series of attacks targeting pro-Kremlin figures.

Overnight Ukraine and Russia exchanged attacks on each other's territories.

Ukrainian authorities said a hospital had been targeted by Russian bombardment.

They added that three people, including a 17-year-old boy, were also killed in attacks across southern Odesa and Zaporizhzhia.

Russia said a Ukrainian strike on an industrial facility in the central Samara region killed four people.

And in the southern Volgograd region another four died after an industrial zone was hit by drones. A further person died in the Bryansk border region, an area that is often fired upon.

Ukraine say these are retaliatory attacks over Russia's persistent targeting of its cities.

This week has seen informal peace talks in Dublin at a military airbase.

US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff earlier had spoken with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow.

On Friday, Taoiseach Micheál Martin said that European voice could not be confined to just member states - paving the way for the UK to have a role.

Ahead of an informal meeting of the EU Council, he said: "The discussions today will focus perhaps both on the content and the type of peace that Europe wants to secure, the sustainable peace, and then also in terms of there will be discussion, obviously, in terms of who represents Europe."

Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelensky has welcomed the pledge of European involvement.

Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022 and about a fifth of the country is now under occupation.

On Thursday Prime Minister Andy Burnham said that UK national security adviser Jonathan Powell would join Zelensky, Witkoff and Kushner for talks in Dublin.

But hours later Downing Street said they had been delayed, which meant that the national security adviser could no longer join the meetings.

articles.title: Owain Wyn Evans completes Children in Need bike ride in Cardiff
articles.summary: Owain Wyn Evans cycled almost 400 miles, setting off from Glasgow and finishing in Cardiff.
articles.body:
Presenter Owain Wyn Evans has completed his challenge of cycling through all four UK nations to raise money for BBC Children in Need.

The Welsh host of BBC Radio 2's Early Breakfast Show rode almost 400 miles , setting off from Glasgow and finishing in Cardiff on Friday.

The challenge started on 9 November in Scotland and over the next five days, Owain rode through Northern Ireland, England and Wales and raised £3,853,530 in the process.

Reflecting on his journey, he said: "This has been the hardest challenge of my life, 100%.

"I can't believe I'm here. It's overwhelming, all the love and passion and commitment people have shown."

The BBC said Owain's challenge would be the "greatest-ever distance" covered in a Radio 2 endeavour for the charity.

He crossed the finish line in Cardiff's Central Square just after 11:00 GMT, and was greeted by a crowd cheering him on before he was met by his husband, Arran Rees.

Owain, 42, whose bike was named Shania Chain, and decked out in Children in Need colours - Pudsey's favourite yellow with coloured spots - said: "Thank you so much everyone, from me and Shania.

"Honestly, this has felt so far away for such a long time. I can't believe that I'm here with this welcome and the sun's out."

Hollywood actor Luke Evans announced the route to Owain each day on BBC Radio 2.

During the 640km feat, he was also surprised with the premiere of Steps' brand-new version of their debut hit 5, 6, 7, 8, retitled 5, 6, 7, donate, which featured new lyrics and extra vocals.

It was recorded to help boost Owain's spirits on the longest day of his challenge.

When the challenge was announced, Owain, who is originally from Ammanford, Carmarthenshire, said: "I'm ready to give it absolutely everything I've got."

He said colleagues Sara Cox, Paddy McGuinness and Vernon Kay had previously achieved "extraordinary things" for Children in Need so he ad "a lot to live up to".

Owain was undertaking his second challenge for the BBC charity fundraiser, following his 24-hour drumathon in 2021 .

During the ride Owain received a heartwarming message of support from his primary school teacher Cath Adams.

Speaking to his parents on Radio 2, he recalled having a pink Care Bears lunch box while in reception because he loved the programme.

He said some classmates laughed at him and it prompted his "first feeling of shame", so he hid his lunchbox.

He added: "I remember Cath Adams bringing it out and telling the other kids that this is alright.

"And she was probably, probably my first ally. And I never realised at the time but I love you Cath Adams, you're amazing."

Asked how he was feeling, Owain said: "There are so many children who need our help and who will be helped by all the donations."

Speaking to Kay, he spoke about the gruelling nature of the challenge.

"You train so hard, me and Shania Chain going around the streets, but the reality of it, it's so hard.

"It's been amazing every step of the way and that's been super emotional as well."

Owain previously admitted he "never enjoyed exercise at school" because of bullying, ahead of his four nations biking challenge.

The broadcaster also expressed his gratitude for the support of Radio 2 listeners.

His messages of support from public figures included one from the Princess of Wales, who recorded a message for him in Welsh, saying: "Hi Owain, it's Catherine, you're doing so well. Keep going. Wishing you all the very best."

Shania Twain was so impressed that the bike had been named after her that she sent a message of good luck before the challenge.

She said: "Hi Owain, Shania Twain here. You're about to take on an incredible challenge for BBC Children in Need, cycling 400 miles through all four nations.

"As you set off in Glasgow, I just want to say: 'Let's Go, Owain!' We'll be cheering you on all the way. Good luck."

She sent him another message when he finished, saying: "Congratulations on completing your incredible challenge for Children in Need. You're still the one my friend, sending you all my love."

Helen Thomas, head of Radio 2, said: "Owain truly captured the hearts of the nation this week as he battled through his epic four nations Challenge.

"On behalf of all the Radio 2 listeners as well as the thousands of children and families who will benefit from his Herculean fundraising efforts we simply can't thank him enough. Diolch Owain! "

Evans began his broadcasting career in Welsh-language television when he presented the children's news programme Ffeil.

He later presented the weather on BBC Wales Today and began hosting BBC Radio 2's Early Breakfast Show in 2023.

articles.summary: A 170-member Indian military contingent has departed for Sri Lanka to participate in the 12th edition of the joint military exercise Mitra Shakti 2026,
articles.body: A 170-member Indian military contingent has departed for Sri Lanka to participate in the 12th edition of the joint military exercise Mitra Shakti 2026, scheduled from November 13 to 26.According to the ministry of defence, the contingent comprises primarily troops from a battalion of the Rajputana Rifles, along with personnel from other arms and services and the Indian Air Force. The exercise will be held at the Army Training School in Maduru Oya, Sri Lanka.The Rajputana Rifles is one of the oldest infantry regiments of the Indian Army, with a history spanning more than 250 years. The regiment has previously participated in Mitra Shakti, including the 10th edition held in Sri Lanka in August 2024.Mitra Shakti is an annual bilateral military exercise conducted alternately in India and Sri Lanka. It aims to strengthen interoperability between the two armies and enhance their ability to conduct joint counter-terrorism operations in semi-urban environments.The 2026 edition will involve joint operational planning and tactical drills, including urban patrolling, vehicle convoy protection, area ambushes, crowd dispersal and combined arms operations against fortified positions.The exercise will conclude with a joint validation exercise in which troops from both countries will demonstrate the operational tactics and procedures practised during the training.India-Sri Lanka military cooperation through such exercises is aimed at strengthening defence ties, improving coordination between the armed forces and contributing to regional security.

articles.title: Quote of the Day by Plato: “Wise men speak because they have something to say; fools because they have to say something.”
articles.summary: Since childhood, we have all been taught to \"think before you speak.\" In adulthood, the lesson becomes more important as people often forget it.
articles.body: Since childhood, we have all been taught to "think before you speak." In adulthood, the lesson becomes more important as people often forget it. While some people speak because they have something meaningful to contribute to the conversation, some only speak because they want to. They either want their word to have more value or they cannot bear the silence. In a world where everyone has an opinion, every moment feels like an obligation to give a reaction, and silence is sometimes mistaken for weakness.Ancient Greek philosopher and Father of Political Philosophy, Plato, said, “Wise men speak because they have something to say; fools because they have to say something.” The quote has not lost its relevance in the modern world, where the internet has provided a space to say things in a moment, without giving much thought.The quote stays as a reminder that the one who speaks the most or the quickest is not always the wisest in the room. It is the ability to pause, reflect and speak only when it is truly required. It forces us to reflect on our own conversations and be more thoughtful about what we speak.The deeper meaning: Wisdom is knowing when words matterThe quote is not a criticism of people who talk too much; rather it is about how much thought people are putting into their speech.A wise person does not need complicated vocabulary or long speeches to convey their message. For them, a few sentences that hold observation, experience or genuine understanding are enough to communicate with their audience. They understand that they only have to speak when they have something worth adding to a conversation, not merely to make their presence felt.On the other hand, the need to say something all the time can sometimes come from insecurity. People who interrupt others often seek attention for themselves at moments when it is not warranted. They tend to provide unsolicited advice and express opinions on matters that are sometimes not even part of the discussion. This reflects their lack of respect for other people's right to speak.There is also an important difference between being silent and having nothing to contribute. Silence does not always mean ignorance, just as speaking confidently does not always mean knowledge. Sometimes, the person who listens carefully understands more than the one who is busy preparing their next response.The real wisdom lies in recognising this difference. It is not about becoming quiet or avoiding conversations. It is about giving our words some thought before allowing them to leave our mouths.Why this quote feels especially relevant in the age of social mediaWe live in a time when having a voice has never been easier. A single post, comment, video or message can reach thousands of people within minutes. Everyone has a platform, and almost every event invites an immediate reaction.But does having the opportunity to speak mean we always need to use it?Social media has created a culture of instant opinions where people form views before understanding the full story. They join online arguments without knowing the context or checking whether the information is true or not. The pressure to be politically woke has led people to speak mindlessly instead of actually being aware.The quote becomes a reminder that we can choose to speak on matters that are important to us, provide opinions on subjects that we know about, and recognise that disagreements are a natural part of dialogue. While there is nothing wrong with expressing opinions, a democracy requires healthy discussions even more. They are essential for the evolution of society, where the highest act of political participation is speech. To achieve this, we need to stop adding to the noise and have an open mind even while having discussions online.The importance of listening before speakingOne of the most overlooked aspects of communication is listening. Often, we listen to the other person to answer, not to understand what the other person is trying to say. When someone is speaking, we are already thinking of our counter-argument, our own experience, or the clever reply we want to give.But genuine listening requires patience. It asks us to put our own thoughts aside for a moment and make room for another person's perspective.In a disagreement between two friends, while one keeps interrupting, the other may take time to understand the situation. While the former wants to prove a point, the latter makes an effort to resolve the situation peacefully. We cannot determine which of them is right or wrong, but the willingness to listen creates space for a better conversation.This is also true in everyday life. At work, thoughtful communication can prevent misunderstandings. In relationships, listening can make people feel respected and understood. Even in casual conversations, knowing when to speak and when to let someone else finish can make a considerable difference.Sometimes, the most meaningful thing we can offer another person is not advice, an explanation or a solution. articles.title: In 2019, an 82-year-old Spokane real estate tycoon with dementia rewrote his will to leave his eldest son just $1,000; now a judge has thrown it out, and that son could inherit most of a $600 million estate
articles.summary: A bitter family inheritance dispute involving one of Spokane’s wealthiest property developers has taken a dramatic turn after a judge ruled that two
articles.body: A bitter family inheritance dispute involving one of Spokane’s wealthiest property developers has taken a dramatic turn after a judge ruled that two children financially exploited their father while he was living with dementia and Alzheimer’s disease. The decision could leave his eldest son in control of a fortune estimated at nearly $1 billion, according to The Spokesman-Review, with further details reported by Moneywise. Spokane County Superior Court Judge Jacquelyn High-Edward ruled on October 26, 2026, in favour of Harley Douglass, who had challenged changes made to his late father Harlan Douglass’ will in 2019. The ruling reinstates an earlier version of the will and disqualifies his younger siblings, Lanzce Douglass and Stacey Douglass Boies, from receiving an inheritance after finding that they had financially exploited their father. Harlan, a prominent real estate developer, died on November 26, 2023, aged 86. His estate was estimated at approximately $600 million, including an extensive property portfolio. However, when disputed assets and other financial interests are taken into account, the wider family fortune has been valued at around $1 billion.The dispute centred on a revised will that dramatically changed how the family wealth would be distributed. Under the 2019 version, Lanzce was entitled to 65% of the estate, while Stacey would receive the remaining 35%. Harley, the eldest of the three siblings, was left with just $1,000. The younger siblings maintained that their father’s decision reflected their renewed relationships with him and took into account the financial support and inheritance Harley had received during his parents’ lifetimes. Harley, however, argued that the changes were made when his father’s cognitive abilities were deteriorating and that his siblings had taken advantage of his vulnerable condition.What the judge found about Harlan’s conditionEvidence presented during the proceedings highlighted the extent of Harlan’s cognitive decline around the time the disputed documents were signed. According to the judge’s findings, Harlan had begun experiencing memory problems years before his death. By 2019, he was struggling with basic financial matters, had difficulty understanding numbers and increasingly depended on other people to read documents, arrange appointments and manage his medication.The court also examined how the paperwork affecting his estate had been prepared and presented to him. The judge found that Lanzce and Stacey had arranged for their father to sign documents they had prepared themselves, without adequately explaining the terms and their financial implications.The circumstances surrounding these transactions raised serious concerns about whether Harlan had been in a position to understand the decisions he was making. After considering the testimony, financial records and other evidence presented during the trial, High-Edward concluded that the siblings had exercised undue influence over their father.Why the siblings could lose their entire inheritanceThe ruling went beyond overturning the disputed will. The judge also invalidated promissory notes worth approximately $155 million that had been issued in favour of Lanzce, Stacey and their five children. These documents represented substantial financial commitments from Harlan.Additionally, the court cancelled property assignments that had transferred real estate interests to the younger siblings. An important factor in the decision was Washington state’s law concerning the financial exploitation of vulnerable adults. Under the legislation, individuals found to have financially exploited someone who later dies cannot benefit from that person’s estate. Consequently, Lanzce and Stacey could be barred from receiving any inheritance from their father, rather than simply losing the advantages created by the revised will.A previous inheritance dispute had already divided the familyThe latest judgment is not the first time the Douglass family has faced a courtroom battle over an inheritance. A similar dispute followed the death of Harlan’s wife, Maxine Douglass, in 2016. Her 2008 will had allocated 50% of the children’s share of her estate to Harley, 40% to Stacey and 10% to Lanzce, while the remaining portion was placed in a trust for Harlan.However, in 2019, Lanzce arranged for a document later known as the Hamilton Deed to be prepared, which altered the distribution of Maxine’s assets and removed Harley as a beneficiary. Harley challenged the arrangement, and in 2023, Spokane County Superior Court Judge Raymond Clary ruled in his favour. The court found that the documents had been used as part of an attempt to disinherit him. The latest decision has therefore added another major chapter to a family dispute that has stretched across several years and involved hundreds of millions of dollars.Could Harley Douglass inherit the entire fortune?For now, Harley appears to be in the strongest position to take control of his father’s estate. His attorney, Steve Hassing, has indicated that the ruling could ultimately leave him with the entire inheritance. However, the final distribution is not yet settled. The court may still need to determine whether the children of Lanzce and Stacey can receive anything under the reinstated 2018 will, despite their parents being disqualified.Lanzce and Stacey’s legal team has also indicated that an appeal remains a possibility. According to subsequent reporting by The Spokesman-Review, the siblings’ attorneys later notified the other parties of their intention to appeal. What began as a dispute over a will that left one son with just $1,000 has now become a legal battle over a family fortune that could approach $1 billion.You use AI every day. articles.title: Maria Bartiromo and her husband bought a five-level New York townhouse for $6.5 million in 2007; nearly 19 years later, the former Fox News host has sold it for $7 million after leaving the network
articles.summary: Maria Bartiromo and her husband, financier Jonathan Steinberg, have sold their five-storey townhouse on the Upper East Side of Manhattan for $7 million.
articles.body: Maria Bartiromo and her husband, financier Jonathan Steinberg, have sold their five-storey townhouse on the Upper East Side of Manhattan for $7 million. They made just $500,000 more than the $6.5 million they paid for the property nearly 19 years ago. The sale took place privately on October 30, 2026, about two months after Fox News Media ended its relationship with the longtime television anchor. Property records cited by Realtor.com and commercial real estate tracker Traded confirm that the single-family home at 213 East 62nd Street was sold in an all-cash deal.According to Traded, the buyers were a trust linked to automotive industry executive Peter Morse and his wife, Gina. The contract was signed on October 5, and the sale was completed 25 days later. Business publication Crain's New York Business noted that this was much faster than the month or more usually needed to complete townhouse sales in Manhattan. Bartiromo and Steinberg do not appear to have publicly listed the property before selling it. Bartiromo, 59, and Steinberg, who is the chief executive of asset management firm WisdomTree, first bought the 3,700-square-foot home for $6.5 million in 2007. However, when adjusted for inflation, that purchase price would be worth about $10.5 million in 2026 dollars, Crain's New York Business reported. This means the couple actually lost money on the sale when inflation is taken into account.Inside the East 62nd Street propertyWhen the couple bought the property in 2007, The New York Observer reported that the five-storey home had five bedrooms, a 32-foot-long kitchen, and a wet bar between the dining room and drawing room on the second floor. The property also had a second-floor balcony overlooking a 39-foot-long backyard garden. Other features included a built-in security system and monitor. According to Traded's sales records, the $7 million sale price works out to $1,892 per square foot for the 3,700-square-foot home.Timing follows abrupt Fox News exitThe sale comes shortly after a major change in Bartiromo's television career. On September 3, 2026, Fox News Media announced that she was leaving the network after more than 12 years. "We thank Maria for her work over the last 12 ½ years and wish her all the best on her next chapter," Fox News Media said in its official statement. According to Realtor.com, Bartiromo had not appeared on any Fox News Media programmes since August 9. The Los Angeles Times reported that the network's decision to part ways with the anchor, who reportedly earned around $6 million a year, was "a business decision". Bartiromo's lawyer later denied claims that she had been fired, according to The Guardian and Crain's New York Business.Bartiromo joined Fox in 2014 after spending about 20 years at CNBC. During her time at the network, she hosted three programmes: "Mornings with Maria," "Maria Bartiromo's Wall Street," and "Sunday Morning Futures". After her departure, Fox brought in different presenters on a rotating basis. These included Larry Kudlow, who temporarily filled in for her. The network also changed the names of two programmes to "Mornings with FOX Business" and "FBN's Wall Street".A week after Fox announced her departure, Bartiromo addressed her viewers on Instagram on September 10. "Before too much time passes, I want to thank all of my friends, followers, and supporters for all of the kind words. I am so grateful for the outpouring of love this week on social media and through texts," she wrote. Her departure also attracted public comments from political figures. On September 3, President Donald Trump posted a message on Truth Social. He wrote: "I can't believe Maria Bartiromo is no longer going to have her great show(s) on FoxNews/Business. Three different shows, always number one. Maria is a total professional, and a true warrior. Her fans, of which there are many, will not be happy. God bless you, Maria!"Ties to New York remain unclearBartiromo has not announced where she will work next on a permanent basis. Selling the Manhattan home where she lived for many years may point to a change in her personal life. However, she has spoken in the past about her strong connection to New York. In a 2019 interview with Resident magazine, Bartiromo spoke about growing up in Brooklyn and working at her family's restaurant. Her grandfather had opened the restaurant after moving from Italy in 1919. "I grew up in Brooklyn and I love New York because of its diversity. articles.body: RANCHI: Police on Friday registered an FIR against Congress MLA from Simdega, Bhushan Bara, under the Pocso Act after a 14-year-old girl alleged that he sexually assaulted her at his residence in Ranchi.Hatia DSP Neeraj Kumar said the girl alleged the incident took place on Aug 5. “She claimed that she was brought from Simdega by the MLA’s wife and her sister in July to enrol her in a school and on Aug 5, the MLA raped her. If something as she has alleged had truly happened, she would have told her parents and taken action against me. She had also accused the MLA’s family members of assault, verbal abuse and physical and mental harassment,” Sahu said.Jharkhand Congress media in-charge Rakesh Sinha said, “Before pointing fingers at others, BJP must introspect on itself and respond to serious allegations raised against BJP functionaries. articles.title: In 1957, Tulsa sealed a brand-new Plymouth in a concrete vault; 50 years later, it emerged waterlogged and rusted after water flooded its underground tomb
articles.summary: Discover the intriguing story of Tulsa's buried Plymouth Belvedere, which emerged after 50 years in a concrete vault, only to find itself waterlogged and rusted. Explore the outcomes of this bold time capsule project from 1957.
articles.body: Most of us have probably put something away somewhere safe only to find it spoiled years later. Now imagine that idea stretching across half a century. In 1957, Tulsa, Oklahoma, residents buried a brand-new Plymouth Belvedere and planted a big reveal for 50 years down the road. CBS News wrote in June 2007, citing an Associated Press report, that hundreds watched as a crane lifted the car out of a 12-by-20-foot concrete vault. However, the car that came out was not the dream machine that they had hoped for.A city party with a car at its centre The car was part of Tulsarama, the city's celebration of 50 years of Oklahoma statehood. The Belvedere burial was a last-minute addition to a planned time capsule, and the Museum of Tulsa History called it a publicity stunt. However, precautions were taken. All fluids were removed from the car. Special materials were designed to coat and protect it before it went into a sealed concrete vault. There was also a contest. Contestants had to predict the number of people who would live in Tulsa in 2007. The winning entry would get the car, and the AP noted that the winner's descendants could also claim it. The museum went on to explain that all the entries were sealed along with the car so everything would be found together.A vault built to lastCBS described the vault as supposedly strong enough to survive a nuclear strike. The car was covered in three layers of protective material. The trunk also held separate containers of gasoline and oil so the car would run even if fuel was no longer available. Even the contents of a woman's handbag went in the glove compartment. It contained 14 bobby pins, a bottle of tranquilliser, lipstick, a pack of gum, tissues, cigarettes, matches, and $2.43. It's those little things that make the story feel so human. The people of 1957 were leaving behind a message for strangers in 2007.The big reveal went wrong Before the lift, officials had already pumped several feet of water out of the vault. A follow-up AP report in The Spokesman-Review recounted how the wrapping, covered with red mud, was removed at a ceremony at the Tulsa Convention Center in front of thousands of people. Under it was a car which was completely covered in rust and would not start. Boyd Coddington, a hot rod builder, was supposed to start the engine. Instead, he said, “She's a mess.” Some items, however, did survive. Around the doors and front fender, there was still some shiny chrome. Workers even managed to pump air into the tyres. The time capsule, buried along with the car, did much better than its neighbour. From it, the organisers pulled out an unfaded American flag, as well as documents, aerial maps and postcards, which were in good condition.Why water is bad news for metal The damage can be explained by basic chemistry. The National Park Service graphic, When the Rust Settles, calls salty air, oxygen, and moisture the main enemies of metal objects. It adds that paint can protect metal, but all paint eventually ends up cracking, and water gets into the cracks. The result is the red powder we call rust. Hence, the metal car did so badly in a vault that had been under several feet of water. Tulsa’s gamble didn't work out as anyone had hoped, but the story goes on. Even a thick concrete vault and careful wrapping couldn’t keep the water out. But still, the people behind it were bold enough to leave something for the future, and that might be the real prize.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: From Australian chana to Canadian masoor: NITI Aayog flags India's food import dependence
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: India may not yet be fully secure in meeting its food requirements, with heavy dependence on imports for essential commodities such as edible
articles.body: NEW DELHI: India may not yet be fully secure in meeting its food requirements, with heavy dependence on imports for essential commodities such as edible oils and pulses, NITI Aayog vice-chairman Ashok Kumar Lahiri said on Friday.Speaking at an event in Delhi, Lahiri said India imports more than half of its edible oil requirements and relies on other countries for several pulses.He questioned whether the country was sufficiently prepared to deal with disruptions in global supplies and sudden price increases."We are talking about Viksit Krishi in Viksit Bharat in 2047. As we move towards Viksit Bharat at 2047, are we secure regarding our food supply across the various products? Perhaps not as yet," he said.Lahiri said he was surprised to learn that chana (gram) consumed in India comes from Australia, while masoor dal is imported from Australia and Canada. Some pulses also come from Myanmar, African countries and Russia, according to news agency PTI."Now you can ask what is wrong with India importing edible oils or oil seeds from Indonesia, Malaysia, Argentina, Brazil, Russia, and Ukraine, and pulses from Australia, Canada, Myanmar, Africa, and Russia," Lahiri said."The problem is, first, the issue of vulnerability to global supply disruptions or price shocks," he added.India meets more than half of its edible oil demand through imports. These imports are estimated at 17 million metric tonnes, worth around $20 billion, Lahiri said.India is also the world's largest producer and consumer of pulses, accounting for nearly a fourth of global consumption. The country consumes around 25-27 million tonnes of pulses every year."For our dal-chawal or dal-roti, we require pulses and edible oils. Any disruption of supply of these essential commodities or price shock can assume the gravity of a strategic disaster," he said.Lahiri said reducing dependence on imports would require greater focus on domestic production of pulses and edible oils. He pointed to the need to diversify crops and reduce the dominance of wheat and paddy in Indian agriculture.Since pulses and oilseed crops generally require less water, he said, promoting their cultivation could also help address agricultural challenges.The NITI Aayog vice-chairman also stressed the need to reduce and eliminate waste in Indian agriculture.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Omagh bomb carrier was an agent for MI5 and Garda, inquiry told
articles.summary: The Policeman who headed up the investigation told the inquiry the bomb carrier may have been a Garda and MI5 agent.
articles.body:
The detective who led the Omagh bombing investigation has told an inquiry that he believes the man who transported the bomb was an agent for both the UK security services agency MI5 and the gardaí (Irish police).

Retired Ch Supt Norman Baxter gave evidence to the Omagh Bombing Inquiry on Friday.

He said: "As I went through the investigation it became very apparent that an individual was a Garda agent. It became apparent that in one operation there was a high potential that he was jointly handled by the security services."

Baxter said he also believed that intelligence services were aware of the bombers' activity before they carried out the Omagh bombing.

Twenty-nine people, including a woman pregnant with twins, died in the Real IRA bombing in the County Tyrone town on 15 August 1998 - the biggest single atrocity in the Troubles.

Baxter said he "formed the view that Special Branch, the security service and GCHQ (Government Communications Headquarters) knew prior to 15 August 1998 the identities of some if not all of the suspects involved in the Omagh bomb".

"The amount of information they knew I can't assess but yes, they knew."

Baxter told the hearing that there was "significant effort by the Garda to prevent their activities being uncovered".

"The Irish government and particularly the Ministry of Justice, have failed to investigate the Garda operations in the period leading up to Omagh, he added saying he was "saddened" by the "absolute failure" of the police investigation.

"It is very sad. I am very proud of my time in the police but this was a failure at leadership, a failure at government level.

"The Republic and United Kingdom, all the apparatus they had, all the technology, their source network, these people should have been stopped and there has to be a reason why that didn't happen."

He also alleged that the gardaí allowed bombs to be taken across the border into Northern Ireland.

"Some devices were being allowed to travel into Northern Ireland, and then there were other devices which had come into Northern Ireland which the source provided to dissidents and those devices had exploded," he said.

"Did Garda officers commit a criminal offence which could be prosecuted in the United Kingdom, that is carrying out an act of terrorism by colluding with dissident republicans, to facilitate the delivery of bombs?

"The government of Ireland had information that a bombing was imminent."

He also told the inquiry about a test run of the bomb route was taken by two "known dissidents" the day before the bombing.

Senior counsel to the inquiry Paul Greaney KC, who was reading from Baxter's report, outlined how the detective noted a vehicle bearing the registration number of Seamus McKenna's car was recorded entering the Thiepval military base in Lisburn in September 1997.

It then re-emerged on the system on 12 August 1998 and was recorded crossing the border at Aughnacloy on 14 August, the day before the bombing.

Another vehicle also travelled the route, it was linked to Liam Campbell, he continued.

When asked about the report, Baxter added: "It might have been a test run in terms of timing how long it took from the origins of the bomb to the target site."

Baxter said he concluded that the Omagh bombers had "free rein" from the middle of 1997 and the authorities allowed that to continue.

"There were a number of opportunities in the past when this group could have been disrupted," he said.

He said he felt guilt about having knowledge of the bombing that he was unable to share with the victims and families.

"I sat for many meetings with various victims' groups and I listened to what they were saying about Garda collusion.

"I listened to what they were saying about Garda knowledge, but Irish government cover ups, and everything in the north and I knew they were telling the truth but legally I couldn't tell them, and I have to pay great respect to the effort that has brought the victims to this place where there is a legal forum where the truth can be told without fear of prosecution.

"It's such a tragedy that we are here when this could have been resolved."

'They could have saved the lives in Omagh'

Later, Baxter said known members of the Provisional IRA were seen with the car the bomb was in at a GAA club in County Armagh the night before the bombing.

The Provisional IRA were on a ceasefire when the attack happened.

"Probably difficult for the families to hear this but that was the major missed opportunity that senior republican figures were with the bomb the night before and they did nothing."

He said the bomb was in a maroon Vauxhall Cavalier at Cullaville GAA club where "senior members of the republican movement" saw the car.

"There were members of the Provisional IRA present with the bomb the night before.

"That is the only definitive point that I know that the bomb could have been stopped in Northern Ireland.

"If one of those people had have called the security forces and said X and X, both are identified, have a bomb because they knew there was a bomb, there was a discussion about the bomb, and they could have stopped it.

"They could have saved the lives in Omagh."

He also said that he cannot rule out that there was a second informer involved in the bombing.

"It is probably not safe to assume it was just one informer in the context of this bomb.

Baxter said the investigation was resourced well.

He said it was a "balancing act" but that he had sufficient people and resources and he was never once questioned about the budget needed to investigate the bombing.

Three days after the attack, the Real IRA released a statement claiming responsibility for the explosion.

It apologised to "civilian" victims and said its targets had been commercial.

No-one has been convicted of carrying out the murders by a criminal court.

In 2009, Michael McKevitt, Liam Campbell, Colm Murphy and Seamus Daly were all ordered to pay a total of £1.6m in damages to the relatives, but appeals against the ruling delayed the compensation process.

A fifth man, Seamus McKenna, was found not liable in the civil action and later died in a roofing accident in 2013.
