articles.title: At 9, Virginia's Ledger Mann used $100 from his piggy bank to create emergency comfort kits for children with autism; more than 475 bags have reached first responders in six states, earning him TIME's Kid of the Year
articles.summary: A nine-year-old boy from Virginia has been named TIME's 2026 Kid of the Year for creating emergency comfort kits for children with autism.
articles.body: A nine-year-old boy from Virginia has been named TIME's 2026 Kid of the Year for creating emergency comfort kits for children with autism. Ledger Mann started the initiative after hearing about a search for a missing child with autism. The incident made him think about how frightening emergencies could be for children who struggle with unfamiliar surroundings, loud sounds and bright lights.Ledger's father, JT Mann, is a sergeant with the Prince George County Police Department. After returning from a search operation, he told his family about a boy who had gone missing. The child was eventually found hiding inside a storage cabinet beneath a gas grill on the back deck of his home.The boy had autism and sensory-processing challenges. First responders had searched the surrounding area with police officers, firefighters, a drone and search dogs before finding him. JT had used a video on his phone to get the child's attention and help him feel less afraid.Ledger, who also has autism, understood how overwhelming the experience could have been. “I felt a little sad for him,” Ledger said, as quoted by Time. “I felt a little bad for him.”How Ledger came up with the ideaAfter hearing his father's account, Ledger began thinking about what could help children with autism feel safer during emergencies. He suggested that first responders should carry bags containing items that could comfort children during stressful situations.His list included blankets, soft toys, books, fidget spinners, wireless headphones and sunglasses. He also suggested keeping a dry-erase board and marker for children who are nonverbal and may find it difficult to communicate.Ledger wanted the items to be kept in a clear backpack so children could see what was inside and point to what they needed. “Dad,” he told his father, “you don’t have those things.”His mother, Amanda Mann, said Ledger developed the entire concept in about 10 minutes. She and JT, along with Ledger's elder brother Peyton, 16, decided to help turn his idea into reality.$100 from his piggy bank helped start the projectLedger's savings became the first source of money for the initiative. He had around $100 in his piggy bank, as he regularly saved money and did not like spending it.The amount was enough to purchase supplies for the first four bags, including soft toys and other comfort items. The family delivered them to local police stations and fire stations. The positive response from first responders encouraged Ledger to prepare more.However, his savings could not support the growing project. His father approached local organisations and community groups for help.The family received donations from churches, the Moose Lodge, the Fraternal Order of Police and other civic organisations. The items were kept affordable, with most purchases made from Dollar Tree and Dollar General stores.JT said the bags did not contain expensive products and that even the headphones cost around $5.Ledger also took responsibility for packing the bags. He carefully checked the contents and made sure every item was arranged properly and remained visible.More than 475 bags distributed across six statesThe family initially distributed the bags across Dinwiddie County, which covers 286 square miles. They placed them at central locations so emergency responders could access them without travelling long distances.Hospitals, emergency medical services teams, police departments and fire departments began keeping the bags at their locations.The initiative soon attracted attention beyond the county. A local television report earlier this year brought requests and offers of support from individuals, companies and first-responder groups in Florida, New York, Maryland, West Virginia, North Carolina and other parts of Virginia.A woman even travelled from Texas to Virginia to deliver bags donated by her company and meet Ledger.So far, the family has assembled and distributed more than 475 bags across six states. They have also created a Facebook page called LGM Bags, named after Ledger Greyson Mann. The family is looking to register the initiative as a 501(c)(3) nonprofit organisation.Soft toys are the most popular itemsChildren who receive the bags during emergencies can choose and keep any item that comforts them. First responders take back the remaining contents and the backpack, replacing the items that have been used.Soft toys have emerged as the most popular comfort items. Ledger's mother said stuffed animals can help children feel safe, regardless of their gender.The family also visits communities that request the bags, delivering completed kits and helping local groups assemble more. These visits allow Ledger to meet first responders and see how his initiative is helping children.One participating area, Ulster County in New York, has committed to assembling 100 bags. The family arranged a Zoom meeting so Ledger could explain how they should be packed.Ledger continues to attend school and enjoy his hobbies, including Lego, jujitsu and football. He has also expressed interest in becoming a police officer, builder or working with robotics.The family hopes to expand the initiative across the country. “I want to have this go everywhere,” Ledger said. “To all of America!”You use AI every day. articles.title: A Mississippi father said his once $800,000 bank account was depleted and he could not pay $600 monthly child support; an appeals court overturned the payment order but left decisions about visits with the mother
articles.summary: A father's financial circumstances became a central issue in a child-support dispute after he told a Mississippi court that an account once holding
articles.body: A father's financial circumstances became a central issue in a child-support dispute after he told a Mississippi court that an account once holding approximately $800,000 had been drained, leaving him homeless and without a regular income. Despite his claims that he could no longer afford payments, a judge ordered him to pay $600 a month for his young son. The father challenged the amount, arguing that the court had not properly established his ability to pay.In an opinion issued on November 10, 2026, available on Justia, the Mississippi Court of Appeals reversed the child-support order and sent the issue back to the lower court for a fresh calculation. However, the appeals court upheld a separate arrangement allowing the child's mother to decide whether and when the father could visit their son.Father said his $800,000 account had been depletedWilliam McLain and Tristan Davis were never married but had a son, identified in court documents as K.D., who was born in May 2023. In December 2023, the Mississippi Department of Human Services filed a complaint seeking to establish paternity and determine child support. Davis subsequently filed a petition requesting custody, supervised visitation and financial support.A September 2024 temporary order granted Davis physical and legal custody of the child and directed McLain to pay $350 a month in child support through the Department of Human Services. At a final hearing in March 2025, the court increased the monthly payment to $600. McLain challenged the decision, saying his financial circumstances did not support such an obligation.During the hearing, the parties discussed bank records showing that McLain had once held approximately $800,000 in a Trustmark account. He described the money as a gift from a friend and said he had supported himself with it for several years. However, he claimed the account had since been depleted, largely because of his gambling addiction. Davis questioned his explanations about the money's origin, saying he had given different accounts involving his grandmother, friends, Bitcoin and stocks.McLain also testified that he had not held a regular job for nine years, had limited education and was now homeless. He said he had previously taken odd jobs, including cutting grass, but could no longer continue because of a back injury.Why the appeals court overturned the $600 orderThe appeals court found that the lower court had not adequately explained how it arrived at the $600 monthly payment. Under Mississippi law, child support for one child is generally calculated using 14% of the parent's adjusted gross income. Courts can depart from these guidelines in appropriate circumstances, but they must explain their reasoning. The law also requires judges to gather sufficient information before imputing income to a parent who is unemployed or has no established earnings. Relevant considerations can include assets, education, health, employment history, job skills and local employment opportunities.In McLain's case, his financial declaration listed no income and showed $31,000 in credit card debt. Although the chancellor referred to substantial deposits and withdrawals in his bank account, the actual statements were not included in the appellate record. The appeals court said there was no reliable way to verify the financial information or determine how the lower court calculated his ability to pay. It therefore reversed the $600 child-support order and remanded the issue for a more detailed assessment based on the statutory requirements.Mother retained control over visitationMcLain also challenged the arrangement allowing Davis to determine visitation at her sole discretion. He argued that the decision effectively denied him access to his son. The lower court had cited his lack of meaningful participation in the proceedings, unemployment, homelessness and absence of an established relationship with the child, who was younger than three at the time.The appeals court majority upheld the arrangement, noting that McLain had not formally requested a specific visitation schedule or proposed conditions under which visits could take place. It said the arrangement gave him an opportunity to establish a relationship with his son and allowed him to return to court if Davis unreasonably refused visitation.However, Presiding Judge Wilson dissented on this issue, arguing that giving the mother complete discretion effectively denied the father an enforceable right to visit his child. He said the evidence did not establish that supervised visitation would pose an imminent risk of harm. His dissent was joined by four other judges: Westbrooks, Lawrence, McCarty and Weddle.What happens nextThe November 10 ruling affirmed the visitation decision but reversed and remanded the child-support issue for further proceedings. It did not eliminate McLain's obligation to support his son; the lower court must determine an appropriate amount using sufficient financial evidence.The case highlights the distinction between a parent's financial responsibility and visitation rights, with both decisions requiring courts to consider the child's best interests and the evidence presented.You use AI every day. articles.title: Meet Lucas Marshall, 17, and Jonah Marshall, 15, of Palm Bay, Florida, who used a paddleboard and kayak after 911 could not reach their flooded neighbours, rescuing a mother, her 11-year-old son and 3 dogs
articles.summary: When Brittany Grant realised the water outside her Palm Bay, Florida, home was no longer staying outside, she and her 11-year-old son Nikoa climbed onto
articles.body: When Brittany Grant realised the water outside her Palm Bay, Florida, home was no longer staying outside, she and her 11-year-old son Nikoa climbed onto the kitchen counter and waited for help. Emergency services could not reach them, so Grant posted a plea for assistance online. That message was seen by neighbour Stephanie Fanguy, who sent her teenage sons, 17-year-old Lucas Marshall and 15-year-old Jonah Marshall, into the floodwaters with an inflatable paddleboard and a borrowed kayak, according to Good News Network and The Washington Post.What followed was a small, improvised rescue that depended on courage, quick thinking, and the willingness of neighbours to act before conditions became worse. Lucas and Jonah reached Grant’s flooded home, helped Nikoa out through a kitchen window, and eventually brought Grant, her son, and their three dogs to safety. Grant later said that if the community had not come together, she did not know how she and her son would have gotten out.The water kept risingGrant had placed sandbags by her front door, hoping they would be enough to protect her single-story home from the rising water. For a while, it seemed like a reasonable precaution. Then, after several hours, water began moving across the floor and into the house.As the flooding worsened, Grant and Nikoa climbed onto the kitchen counter, watching the water rise around them. The situation became increasingly frightening because the water was not simply inconvenient, it was cutting off normal routes out of the neighbourhood and making it difficult for emergency responders to reach them.Grant called 911, but the operator told her that emergency services were unable to reach her home. With the water continuing to rise and no immediate rescue on the way, she turned to Facebook and posted a video asking anyone nearby for help.A neighbour saw the pleaStephanie Fanguy saw Grant’s online message and immediately understood the urgency. Rather than waiting for authorities or assuming someone else would respond, she mobilised her own sons, Lucas and Jonah, and helped them prepare for a rescue.The brothers did not have specialised flood-rescue equipment. They used an inflatable paddleboard and a borrowed kayak, tools that might normally be associated with a day on the water rather than an emergency. But in that moment, those simple vessels became the difference between being trapped and being able to reach safety.Lucas and Jonah made their way through the flooded streets toward Grant’s home. Their plan was straightforward: get to the house, reach Nikoa, and begin moving people and pets out of danger.Helping a frightened childNikoa, Grant’s 11-year-old son, struggles with anxiety, according to Click Orlando. Being trapped in a rapidly flooding house was already stressful, and being asked to climb out through a kitchen window into uncertain water could have made the situation even more overwhelming.Lucas tried to keep Nikoa calm by speaking with him, asking simple questions, and making light-hearted comments about the weather. It was not a dramatic rescue technique, but it was an important one. A frightened child needed reassurance as much as physical help.The boys guided Nikoa out through the kitchen window and onto the paddleboard or kayak, depending on what was needed at the time. Once Nikoa was safe, they turned their attention to Grant and the family’s three dogs.Dogs, water, and a difficult journeyRescuing three dogs during a flood is not a simple add-on to a human rescue. Animals can panic, resist being lifted or carried, and take up space on an already crowded board or kayak. One of Grant’s dogs reportedly took up half the paddleboard, making the journey back through the flooded neighbourhood even more challenging.Still, Lucas and Jonah kept going. They brought Grant, Nikoa, and all three dogs to safety, completing a rescue that began with a social media post and ended with a family reunited on dry ground.Grant later described the experience as proof that community still matters. “The community came together and saved us,” she said. “If it wasn’t for them, I don’t know how we would have gotten out.” She also said her faith in humanity had been restored, noting that other neighbours had volunteered to help as well.Why the teens actedWhen asked why they went, Jonah gave an answer that was simple and direct. “Because they needed help and they were in trouble and danger, so just didn’t think about it and just went to help them,” he said.That response has resonated with many people who have read about the rescue. The boys did not wait for recognition, calculate the risk, or ask whether someone else was better positioned to help. They saw neighbours in danger and acted.Their mother, Stephanie Fanguy, also played an important role. By seeing the post, taking it seriously, and helping her sons respond, she turned a moment of online distress into a practical rescue effort. The story is not only about two teenagers, it is about a neighbourhood that refused to look away.A flood that overwhelmed a communityThe flooding in Palm Bay was part of a larger weather event that affected communities across Brevard County, including Melbourne and Port St. Lucie. Weather reports described the rainfall as a 1,000-year rain event, a term used to describe rainfall so extreme that it has a very low probability of occurring in any given year.Events like that can overwhelm drainage systems, close roads, and leave residents isolated even when emergency services are trying to respond. In Grant’s case, the water rose quickly enough that waiting for official help became impossible.That is why neighbour-to-neighbour action mattered so much. While formal emergency response is essential, local residents are often the first people able to reach someone in trouble, especially when roads are flooded and conventional vehicles cannot get through.A reminder about preparednessThe rescue is a powerful reminder that flood preparedness is not only about sandbags, insurance, and evacuation routes. It is also about knowing your neighbours, having a way to communicate when phone service or transportation fails, and understanding that help may need to come from unexpected places.Grant’s decision to post online was crucial. It turned a private emergency into a public call for help, allowing nearby residents to see what was happening and respond quickly. In a flooding situation, that kind of communication can save time, and sometimes it can save lives.For Lucas and Jonah, the rescue was not about becoming heroes. It was about doing what needed to be done when someone nearby was in danger. Their actions turned a frightening afternoon into a story of community, courage, and the kind of everyday kindness that can make an enormous difference when people need it most.You use AI every day. articles.title: 20 years after withdrawal, HC restores 81-year-old ex-Serviceman’s increments
articles.summary: Punjab and Haryana HC restores five increments withdrawn from 81-year-old ex-serviceman Randhir Singh, quashes 2005 Punjab govt recovery and pension cuts.
articles.body: Chandigarh: The Punjab and Haryana high court has set aside Punjab govt orders withdrawing five increments granted to an ex-Serviceman and directing recovery of the excess amount.Justice Sudepti Sharma allowed a writ petition filed by Randhir Singh, quashing two orders dated Nov 8 and Nov 23, 2005, which reduced his basic pay from Rs 5,800 to Rs 5,160 and cut his pension benefits shortly after his retirement on Sept 30, 2005.Singh served in the Indian Army from Sept 26, 1963, to September 30, 1978, before joining the Punjab govt as a Daffadar in the SYL canal project. Under an order dated April 24, 1996, he was granted nine increments for his military service. Following an objection raised by the Accountant General on August 18, 2005, the state withdrew five increments linked to the Second National Emergency (1971–1977).The petitioner’s counsel, Ranjivan Singh, contended that the benefit had been wrongly withdrawn. He submitted that a division bench of the high court had stayed recovery pursuant to the impugned orders on Feb 23, 2006. He also pointed out that the petitioner was around 81 years old and sought relief from the court.The state, represented by Punjab deputy advocate general Ravneet S Joshi, contended that the petitioner was entitled to the military service benefit only for the First National Emergency, for which four increments were admissible. The five increments granted to him were not admissible under the amended rules, Joshi argued.The state submitted that the increments had been withdrawn after a review and that a show-cause notice had been issued to the petitioner, who had also filed a reply.While referring to a Punjab govt letter dated July 19, 2001, directing departments to review and withdraw wrongly granted benefits, the high court also noted a subsequent clarification issued by the Department of Defence Services and Welfare on Aug 5, 2002. The policy barred authorities from reopening cases involving emergency benefits granted on or before Oct 13, 1998.The bench observed, “A perusal of the letter dated August 5, 2002, clarifies that the cases of those ex-Servicemen who had been granted the benefit of military service up to October 13, 1998, were not to be reconsidered in view of the judgment passed by the Hon’ble Supreme Court in Chitaranjan Singh Cheema, Junior Sports Officer and another versus Government of Punjab and others, 1997 (1) SLR 697. The petitioner was granted the benefit of military service before October 13, 1998; therefore, his case could not be reconsidered.”Accordingly, the high court allowed the writ petition and set aside the orders dated Nov 8 and Nov 23, 2005.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Chandigarh | Silver Rate in Chandigarh | Bank Holidays in Chandigarh | Public Holidays in Chandigarh | Chandigarh AQI | Weather in Chandigarh | Petrol Price in Chandigarh | Diesel Price in Chandigarh | CNG Price in Chandigarh | LPG Price in ChandigarhStay updated with the latest Chandigarh news. articles.title: An Arizona woman sleeps in her car when her disability keeps her out of her apartment, but Sedona bans sleeping in vehicles even on private land; a November 12 federal ruling revived her disability lawsuit
articles.summary: A federal appeals court has allowed a disability discrimination lawsuit filed by a woman in Sedona to move forward.
articles.body: A federal appeals court has allowed a disability discrimination lawsuit filed by a woman in Sedona to move forward. The woman sleeps in her car because her severe obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) often makes it impossible for her to enter her own apartment. In a published ruling issued on November 12, 2026, a three-judge panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit found that a lower court judge was wrong to dismiss Sabrina Beram's lawsuit against the City of Sedona under Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA). The decision allows Beram to seek financial compensation and a court order stopping police from enforcing the city's ban on sleeping in vehicles against her when she rests in the parking lot of her apartment complex.According to Ninth Circuit court records, Beram rents an apartment in Sedona, Arizona, and lives with severe, long-term obsessive-compulsive anxiety. When she "perceives unclean conditions in her apartment," she "experiences a strong sensory perception" that feels like "an electric fence" that "commands her not to enter" her home, the court's opinion states. Beram follows cleaning routines "designed to make the unclean conditions tolerable." However, these routines can take several hours and often cannot be completed "within enough time to obtain a restful sleep," according to the ruling written by Circuit Judge Roopali H. Desai. On these nights, which happen at least three times a week, she sleeps in her car in her apartment complex's parking lot. If no parking spaces are available, she sleeps in other public or private places around Sedona.Sedona vehicle ban and police warningsSleeping in a vehicle anywhere in Sedona, even on private property, is against the law under Sedona City Code Section 9.10.010. The law also makes it illegal for private property owners or managers to knowingly allow someone to sleep in a vehicle on their land. Breaking this rule is a class 1 misdemeanor. According to court filings, the punishment can include up to six months in jail, a fine of up to $2,500, or both. However, city rules state that police officers cannot arrest someone for sleeping in a vehicle unless an officer or property owner has first given that person a warning.Sedona police officers have warned Beram on two occasions. During the first incident, she was sleeping in her car at a public trailhead. "A Sedona police officer knocked on her window and told her she had to leave." The officer also told her that he had "put a note in her file" so other officers would know she had already received a warning, the Ninth Circuit noted. During the second incident, an officer woke her while she was sleeping in her car at a park. The officer told her that sleeping in a vehicle was illegal, ordered her to leave, and warned that she would receive a citation if she did not follow the order.Beram's landlord also threatened to end her lease after finding out that she slept in the apartment complex's parking lot. Beram had made two requests for a disability accommodation, but the property manager did not respond to either one. Instead, the manager sent her a lease addendum warning that "[t]he City of Sedona does not permit sleeping in vehicles within the city limits". It also said her lease would not be renewed if she broke the rule. Beram later reached a settlement with the property owner. However, the agreement allows the landlord to cancel it if either party receives a warning or is charged under the city ordinance.City denies exemption under federal disability lawAfter receiving the lease addendum, Beram wrote to the Mayor of Sedona asking for a reasonable accommodation under Title II of the ADA. She wanted the city to make an exception so she could sleep in her car without facing enforcement of the vehicle ban. She later limited her request to the parking area of her apartment complex. The city rejected her requests. Community Legal Services then filed a federal lawsuit on her behalf in the U.S. District Court for the District of Arizona. US District Judge Diane J. Humetewa dismissed Beram's case, saying she did not have enough legal grounds to bring the lawsuit. The judge concluded that receiving two police warnings did not prove that she faced an immediate risk of prosecution. Judge Humetewa also refused to let Beram submit updated versions of her complaint.The Ninth Circuit panel overturned that decision. It included Circuit Judge Ana de Alba and U.S. District Judge Edward M. Chen, who was serving by special appointment. Judge Desai wrote that Beram had shown enough grounds to seek financial damages. Being denied a disability accommodation was itself a real injury, she explained. This was in addition to the emotional distress and lost work time Beram said she had experienced. The appeals court also found that Beram faced a real risk of future enforcement. "The officers' warnings were not mere threats of enforcement: they were the first step of enforcement," Judge Desai wrote. She explained that the warnings met the legal requirement that must be completed before someone can be arrested under the ordinance. The judges also noted that Sedona had issued criminal citations to at least two other people for sleeping in vehicles on private property.Criminal ordinances subject to disability protectionsSedona's lawyers argued that Beram's problem was with her landlord, not the city. They also claimed that Title II of the ADA was never intended to interfere with local criminal laws. Judge Desai rejected both arguments. "This argument ignores that the ordinance criminalizes sleeping on both public and private property," she wrote. "And it prohibits private property owners from allowing someone to sleep in their car on the owner's property." The panel also referred to earlier court decisions involving civil zoning and nuisance rules. It ruled that following local government rules and regulations is a public activity covered by the ADA."Discrimination under Title II may include the failure to provide reasonable accommodation that would allow a person with a disability to comply with a criminal ordinance," Judge Desai stated. As Capitol Media Services reported, Thursday's ruling does not mean Beram has won her lawsuit. The Ninth Circuit sent the case back to the Arizona district court for further proceedings. The appeals court instructed that Beram can file a fifth amended complaint. articles.body: Patna: RJD working president Tejashwi Prasad Yadav on Friday accused the ruling NDA of shielding lawmakers and functionaries whose names have figured in criminal cases involving loot, murder and land grabbing. articles.title: BJP, Shiv Sena and NCP locked in tug-of-war for Satara DCC bank chief’s post
articles.summary: Mahayuti allies BJP, Shiv Sena and NCP clash over Satara DCC Bank chairperson election on Nov 18, with a 21-member board and shifting alliances.
articles.body: Kolhapur: Mahayuti parties — BJP, Shiv Sena and NCP — are once again at loggerheads over the election of the chairperson of the Satara District Central Cooperative Bank, scheduled for Nov 18. Although all three parties are part of the ruling alliance, differences over the bank’s leadership have triggered a fresh political tug-of-war.In the Sangli DCC chairperson election, the Maha Vikas Aghadi has a majority of 11 directors out of 21 on its side. It is now looking to rope in Shiv Sena, which has won three seats in the Sangli DCC, into its arrangement to keep the BJP from inching closer to power.In Satara, the BJP has nine directors, the NCP eight and Shiv Sena four. The 21-member board will elect the chairperson, with the majority mark fixed at 11 in the Satara DCC as well.The contest carries the baggage of a bitter recent past. When the Shiv Sena and NCP combine had a majority to elect the Zilla Parishad president, the BJP managed to win over turncoats from the two parties and ensured its candidate’s victory.Ministers Shamburaj Desai of Shiv Sena and Makarand Patil of the NCP had alleged that they were assaulted by police during the Zilla Parishad president election.Amid this, chief minister Devendra Fadnavis has deployed minister Shivendraraje Bhosale to find a solution and get all three parties together. NCP and Sena are eager to take revenge against BJP, but the extent to which they will succeed is crucial.“I have been asked by the CM to get all local leaders of Mahayuti to sit together and find a way out and if it is not possible then the CM can intervene,” said Bhosale.Bhosale on Thursday night met deputy CM Eknath Shinde at the latter’s Dare Tam house. They both discussed the political situation in Satara DCC. According to sources, Sena and NCP are likely to pitch for their chairperson for the DCC.In Sangli, Sena is moving closer to MVA parties and may secure the vice-chairperson’s post if its three directors support the MVA candidate, sources said.
